title: Dropped Head Syndrome: The Importance of Neurophysiology in Distinguishing Myasthenia Gravis from Parkinson’s Disease
case_prompt:
A 71-year-old man reported a subtle onset of severe neck flexion over several months, which progressively worsened. He also noted mild dysphagia and dysphonia. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, arterial hypertension, and mild cervical spondylosis. His father had Parkinson’s disease; the patient himself did not smoke or drink and took no medications. 

On neurologic examination, he had hypomimia, mild bradykinesia, asymmetric rigidity, and a shuffling gait. There was no ptosis or diplopia. Strength testing revealed 2/5 power in the neck extensors and 5/5 power in all other muscle groups; cognition was intact. 

Brain and cervical spine MRI scans showed no structural abnormalities. Repetitive nerve stimulation of the neck extensors revealed a reduction in the amplitude and area of compound muscle action potentials between the first and fourth stimuli. Needle electromyography did not show any myopathic or neuropathic features. Laboratory testing demonstrated high‐titer acetylcholine receptor–binding antibodies (8 nmol/L; normal <0.40 nmol/L), whereas muscle‐specific kinase antibodies and other markers, including creatine kinase, aldolase, and thyroid‐stimulating hormone, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed no thymoma.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Structural cervical abnormality — “Brain and cervical spine MRI scans were unremarkable, ruling out possible structural abnormalities.”  
2. Myopathic or neuropathic disorder — “The needle EMG exam was not indicative of myopathic or neuropathic features.”  
3. Antecollis from Parkinsonism — “Parkinson’s disease (PD) can present with ... antecollis, which is caused by an increased axial tone of the anterior cervical muscles but without muscle weakness.”  
4. MuSK‐positive myasthenia gravis — “Other laboratory tests ... muscle-specific kinase antibodies ... were within normal limits.”  
5. Myasthenia gravis — “Electromyography (EMG) showed a reduction in the amplitude and area of compound muscle action potentials ... consistent with abnormal neuromuscular transmission.”  
6. Myasthenia gravis confirmation — “high-titer (8 nmol/L) positivity for acetylcholine receptor-binding antibodies ... a hallmark of MG.”
